results.message: My pastor says if I question him I'm questioning God, and I have to prove my faith by obeying him without asking.

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
No. A bishop among us is given a people, and he answers for them. The charge runs both ways: he will be asked what became of them, and they can hold him to it. When one of our own bishops was made bishop, it happened over his reluctance. Pontius wrote: “I think this one fact is enough to prove his good works. By the judgment of God and the favour of the people, he was chosen for the sacred office and the rank of bishop. He was still newly baptized and, as people thought, a beginner. He was still in the first days of his faith, in the untaught season of his spiritual life. Yet a noble nature shone out in him. He did not yet shine with the glow of office, only with the glow of hope. Even so, he gave every promise that he could be trusted with the sacred office coming to him.”

God's judgment and the people's favour together put him in that seat. A pastor among us does not stand above question. He stands under it, because the people he is given can stand in front of his own seat and refuse to leave until he hears them. What you describe is not our bond.

glosses.plain_meaning: We are not a silent audience. We put men into office, and we say so out loud. We can stand in front of a bishop's own seat and refuse to go home.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, 'the people' names the congregation when it acts. They consent, they demand, and they elect -- unlike the flock, which is the congregation being cared for.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener may hear either a passive congregation or a modern democratic electorate with formal voting rights. Neither is right. A corporate body whose consent and demand genuinely constitute a call to office, and which can be exerted disruptively, but which holds no procedural mechanism and can still be refused.
false_friend: a passive congregation with no real leverage over its own clergy
a modern democratic electorate, with a formal ballot and a fixed voting procedure

confidence.divergence_note: Widely Accepted rather than Documented: Pontius's own presence at Curubis is licensed for that specific fact but his own biography generally (SSSS2-4, Cyprian's conversion) has not been independently re-checked this session (lpc.source.pontius-life-and-passion-of-cyprian's own divergence_note).

In the vendored English edition of Cyprian the Latin plebs occurs exactly three times, all inside the 19th-century American editor's own introductory and elucidatory prose, none inside Cyprian's own letters. Cyprian's Latin does use it: Hartel's letters carry plebs in running text, 89 whole-word occurrences with notes excluded, and letter 43 is headed CYPRIANVS PLEBI VNIVERSAE S. 'The people' is the English volume's own recurring rendering for the congregation as an acting body. It is a working handle, and whether plebs becomes the world word is not settled.

The text field is the ANF English as printed. modern_rendering follows Hartel's Latin where the English misleads: 'priesthood' renders sacerdotium, here the bishop's office, given as 'the sacred office'; 'neophyte' renders neophytus, 'newly baptized'; 'novice' renders nouellus, 'a beginner'; and 'a generous disposition' renders generosa indoles, 'a noble nature'.

references.spoken_rendering: I think this one fact is enough to prove his good works. By the judgment of God and the favour of the people, he was chosen for the sacred office and the rank of bishop. He was still newly baptized and, as people thought, a beginner. He was still in the first days of his faith, in the untaught season of his spiritual life. Yet a noble nature shone out in him. He did not yet shine with the glow of office, only with the glow of hope. Even so, he gave every promise that he could be trusted with the sacred office coming to him.
references.speaker: Pontius, our bishop's own deacon

confidence.divergence_note: The text field is the ANF English as printed. modern_rendering follows Hartel's Latin where the English misleads: 'priesthood' renders sacerdotium, here the bishop's office, given as 'the sacred office'; 'neophyte' renders neophytus, 'newly baptized'; 'novice' renders nouellus, 'a beginner'; and 'a generous disposition' renders generosa indoles, 'a noble nature'.
